column4: The section cites Pharaoh’s threat to crucify the magicians on palm trunks and asks who can inflict the more severe, lasting torment; 89:25–26 answers that no human can match God’s punishment or binding.
The magicians answer the threat in 20:71 by limiting Pharaoh’s power to “this worldly life”; that boundary clarifies why his promised torture cannot rival the judgment in 89:25–26.
The magicians answer Pharaoh’s claim that his punishment lasts longer (20:71) with “Allah is better and more enduring” (وَاللَّهُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ), directly reversing his measure of authority.

In Moses’ encounter with Pharaoh, the boast “I am your most exalted lord” (أَنَا۠ رَبُّكُمُ الْأَعْلَىٰ) frames the same human claim of mastery that the section’s peg-owner embodies; 79:25 supplies the answer.

After Pharaoh’s claim in 79:24, God seizes him with the exemplary punishment of the first and later life; this reverses the section’s Pharaoh’s boast that his own punishment can be strongest and lasting.
The section cites the same afterlife inventory: shackles (أَنكَالًا) and blazing fire, a direct parallel to its image of punishment joined to binding.
After saying in 73:15 that a messenger was sent to Pharaoh, this ayah says Pharaoh disobeyed and God seized him with a grievous seizure; it shows the peg-owner’s force ending in God’s stronger grasp.
This repeats the section’s title for Pharaoh, ذُو الْأَوْتَادِ, in a list of earlier peoples who denied messengers, confirming that the epithet belongs to his coercive power and eventual judgment.
The section’s named root و ت د also names mountains as pegs (أَوْتَادًا); this gives the peg image a second Quranic scene, with the grounded mountains rather than a human ruler’s coercive title.

This is the section’s exact word وَثَاق in a battle scene: captives are tightly bound, then may be released or ransomed when fighting ends. Its bounded human restraint contrasts with 89:26’s unmatchable binding.
The section cites the order to seize and shackle the person who received his book in the left hand; this is the first bodily restraint in the punishment sequence continued in 69:31–32.
The section cites this long chain, into which the condemned person is to be put; it makes the binding in 89:26 concrete as an afterlife restraint.
The section explicitly links this failure to urge feeding the poor with 89:18; here it is named as part of the condemned person’s cause, tying the final restraint to neglect of the needy.

The criminal who comes to his Lord has Hell and “neither dies therein nor lives”; in the same passage as Pharaoh’s threat, this makes human, time-bounded torment a poor measure of the lasting punishment in the section.
Pharaoh threatens Moses’ believing magicians with amputation and crucifixion, a repeated human attempt to fasten bodies in punishment against the section’s divine counter-binding.
This parallel account adds Pharaoh’s threat to cut hands and feet from opposite sides before crucifying the magicians; it repeats the bodily fixation behind the section’s peg and lash images.

For those who wage war and spread corruption in the land, this ayah names crucifixion among the penalties; it recalls Pharaoh’s crucifixion threat while placing earthly coercion under a divine boundary and judgment.

The prescribed hundred lashes are a literal bodily striking, connecting to the section’s dictionary explanation that the source root ع ذ ب began with striking; the fixed count also contrasts with 89:25’s unmatchable torment.
This separate offense also receives a measured flogging, eighty lashes; it supplies another bounded human instance of the bodily blow that the section sets beside divine punishment.

The section’s named root ص ب ب appears in the command to pour boiling-water torment over a person’s head (صُبُّوا فَوْقَ رَأْسِهِ مِنْ عَذَابِ الْحَمِيمِ); this is the clearest parallel to a lash of torment poured down as a mass.

The same root ص ب ب describes boiling water poured from above the heads of the disbelieving disputants; it makes the section’s poured punishment a specific Quranic scene, not merely a large single blow.

The next ayah says the boiling water melts what is in their bellies and their skins; this completes the bodily effect of the head-pour in 22:19 and echoes the section’s account of the lash entering skin.
The scene then adds iron maces for the punished group; that separate striking instrument gives a concrete counterpart to the section’s dictionary note that torment originally meant a blow.
Before the head-pour in 44:48, the condemned man is seized and dragged to the midst of Hell; this contributes forced bodily helplessness to the same punishment sequence.
After the pour in 44:48, the sufferer is addressed ironically as “mighty, noble” (الْعَزِيزُ الْكَرِيمُ); the reversal makes worldly force and rank sound as hollow as Pharaoh’s threat.

In Lot’s punishment, stones of baked clay are rained down on the town; this is a literal falling mass that clarifies the section’s image of punishment poured from above, though the falling material is stone rather than a whip.
This parallel account says stones of baked clay were rained upon Lot’s people; it repeats the specific image of a punitive mass descending from above that the section draws from “poured.”

The section’s named root ص ب ب also describes God pouring water abundantly; here the action is provision rather than torment, exposing the striking difference between a life-giving pour and 89:13’s punishment.
The next ayah says the earth is split open after the abundant water of 80:25; that is the soil’s response to the same pour, continuing its life-producing contrast to the section’s destructive mass.
Grain grows from the watered earth; this completes the positive result of the same root’s pouring in 80:25, against the section’s poured lash.

God is said to be able to send punishment from above or below, or make people taste one another’s violence; the vertical descent and multiple forms concretize the section’s “mixed kinds” and mass-from-above image.
On the judgment day, punishment covers people above them and beneath their feet; this gives the section’s poured mass an encompassing, inescapable scene rather than a single point of impact.
The criminals on that day are bound together in shackles (مُقَرَّنِينَ فِي الْأَصْفَادِ), a direct afterlife picture of the binding named in 89:26.
This ayah stages shackles around necks and chains while the condemned are dragged, a direct bodily counterpart to the section’s binding image.
The chained people of 40:71 are then in boiling water and burned in the Fire; it completes the binding-and-punishment scene with heat.
The section cites this pairing of chains, fetters, and blazing fire prepared for disbelievers, another direct Quranic joining of restraint and torment.
People thrown into a narrow place in Hell are described as bound together (مُقَرَّنِينَ); this makes confinement itself part of their punishment, like the section’s unmatchable binding.
Those who deny resurrection are pictured with shackles around their necks and as inhabitants of the Fire; the verse connects rejection to the same bodily restraint and afterlife punishment.
After the weak blame those who led them astray, God places shackles around the disbelievers’ necks; their coercive earthly relation ends in the judgment binding developed by the section.
The neck-shackle image appears here as a figure accompanying the disbelievers’ refusal to believe, not as an afterlife sentence; it shows the same restraint image serving a different function.

The condemned repeatedly receive new skins so they can taste torment; alongside the section’s dictionary account of braided leather entering skin, this makes the body’s surface a site of recurring pain.
Between the taking-and-shackling order in 69:30 and the long chain in 69:32, this ayah orders the person to be roasted in Hell; its own contribution is the fire that joins the restraint sequence.
After Pharaoh threatens crucifixion in 7:124, the magicians say they will return to their Lord; their answer sets the tyrant’s bodily threat against the judgment beyond his control.

The magicians identify their belief as the reason Pharaoh punishes them and ask God for patience and a faithful end; their allegiance makes his torture a temporary coercion rather than ultimate authority.
After the threat in 26:49, the magicians say there is no harm and that they return to their Lord; this gives the same human threat a limit beyond Pharaoh’s reach.
The magicians hope their Lord will forgive them after Pharaoh’s threat; their final appeal places his punishment beside a divine judgment and mercy he cannot control.
This account names Pharaoh’s “evil torment” (سُوءَ الْعَذَابِ) and specifies the slaughter of sons; it shows the earthly violence behind the section’s Pharaoh and his claim to punish.
The reminder of Pharaoh’s “evil torment” and killing of sons repeats the concrete violence behind the peg-owner’s coercive power.

Moses tells his people to recall Pharaoh’s “evil torment,” including slaughtering sons and sparing women; this supplies another Quranic account of the human rule that the section contrasts with God’s punishment.
Pharaoh exalts himself, divides the people, oppresses a group, kills their sons, and is called a corrupter; this joins the section’s peg-owner, tyranny, and corruption in one scene.
After naming Pharaoh among deniers in 38:12, this ayah says each denied the messengers and God’s punishment became due; it completes the peg-owner’s placement among those who meet divine retribution.

Immediately before the cited failure to urge food for the poor in 69:34, this gives unbelief in God as another cause of the punishment; it locates social neglect within the wider judgment in that passage.
The section links 69:34 to 89:18’s failure to urge food for the poor; here hoarding gold and silver without spending in God’s way is likewise tied to painful punishment.
The next ayah turns hoarded gold and silver into heated metal that brands foreheads, sides, and backs; this joins the section’s social indictment to a concrete bodily punishment.
This ayah repeats the section’s specific phrase about not urging food for the poor (وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ), making the condemned omission a repeated Quranic measure of conduct.
Righteousness here includes giving beloved wealth to the needy and freeing those in bondage; these acts reverse both the section’s neglect of the poor and its image of binding.
The righteous feed the poor, orphan, and captive (مِسْكِينًا وَيَتِيمًا وَأَسِيرًا); this reverses the section’s cited failure to urge food even for the poor.
The next ayah says they feed only for God’s sake, seeking neither reward nor thanks; it contrasts care for the captive and poor with the hoarding condemned in the section’s surrounding verses.
Their reason is fear of a grim day; this joins the feeding contrast in 76:8–9 to the final punishment that the section depicts.
Freeing a neck (فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ) is the first act named in the steep path; it directly reverses the section’s binding image.
The next act is feeding people on a day of hunger, a direct reversal of the failure to urge food for the poor cited by the section.
This ayah praises those who urge one another to patience and mercy; it reverses the section’s specific rebuke of those who do not urge care for the needy.

The command not to make one’s hand “chained to the neck” (مَغْلُولَةً إِلَىٰ عُنُقِكَ) pictures hoarding as self-restraint; beside the section’s poor-feeding indictment, it shows binding imagery can describe withheld wealth.

The Prophet is said to remove the burdens and shackles that were upon people; this is a release from restraint, reversing the punishment binding in the section, though the verse’s shackles are figurative religious burdens.
The section’s named root و ث ق appears in the “most trustworthy handhold” (الْعُرْوَةِ الْوُثْقَىٰ); here a secure bond is freely grasped and cannot break, a positive counterpart to coercive binding.

This repeats the “most trustworthy handhold” (الْعُرْوَةِ الْوُثْقَىٰ) for one who submits to God and does good; the source root’s firmness thus also describes chosen reliance rather than imposed restraint.

The section’s named root و ث ق appears in the covenant with which God “bound” the people (وَاثَقَكُم بِهِ); this is a pledged bond rather than a shackle, clarifying the root’s nonphysical sense beside 89:26.
The same root’s covenant sense appears in the breaking of God’s bond after its confirmation; unlike 89:26’s unmatchable binding, this verse pictures humanly severed ties and corruption.
This repeats the confirmed covenant’s breaking and severed relations; the section’s root و ث ق can name a social bond people rupture, a contrast to the final binding no one can match.
